original_question: Call an irreducible component Z of the punctual Hilbert scheme Hilb_d(A^n, 0) smoothable if Z is contained in the smoothable component of Hilb_d(A^n). What can be said about such smoothable components, and how many of them are there for a given pair (n, d)?
target_in_paper: Problem XXIX in §2.7 ("Punctual Hilbert schemes") of Jelisiejew, Open problems in deformations of Artinian algebras, Hilbert schemes and around.
correct_elements: Your draft already matches the paper's target almost verbatim: it asks about irreducible components Z of the punctual Hilbert scheme Hilb_d(A^n,0), uses the paper's notion of a component being smoothable by containment in the smoothable component of the full Hilbert scheme Hilb_d(A^n), and asks both for structural information and for the number of such components for fixed (n,d).
missing_details: The paper works over an algebraically closed field k; this global convention should be stated explicitly to make the question stand-alone (§1.3).

Hilb_d(A^n,0) should be defined explicitly as the punctual Hilbert scheme, i.e. the fiber over d[0] of the Hilbert-Chow morphism, parametrizing length-d subschemes of A^n_k supported at the origin 0 (§1.3).
Hilb_d(A^n) should be identified as the Hilbert scheme of length-d subschemes of affine n-space A^n_k (§1.3).

The smoothable component of Hilb_d(A^n) should be defined explicitly as the closure of the open locus of smooth degree-d subschemes; over an algebraically closed field these are tuples of d reduced points (§2.1).

It should be made explicit that the condition Z is smoothable means Z is viewed inside Hilb_d(A^n) via the natural inclusion Hilb_d(A^n,0) subset Hilb_d(A^n), and is contained in the smoothable component there (§1.3, §2.1, §2.7).
The variables n and d should be quantified as fixed positive integers; the paper does not add any extra characteristic-zero hypothesis here (§1.3, §2.7).

The nearby sentence after Problem XXIX gives motivation: unlike for the full Hilbert scheme, the author knows of no natural injective map from components of the punctual Hilbert scheme to components of the full Hilbert scheme; this is context worth knowing, though it is not part of the formal problem (§2.7).
refined_question: Let k be an algebraically closed field, let Hilb_d(A^n_k) denote the Hilbert scheme of length-d subschemes of affine n-space A^n_k, and let Hilb_d(A^n_k,0) be the punctual Hilbert scheme, i.e. the fiber over d[0] of the Hilbert-Chow morphism, parametrizing length-d subschemes supported at the origin 0. Let R_d^n subset Hilb_d(A^n_k) be the smoothable component, namely the closure of the locus of smooth length-d subschemes of A^n_k. Call an irreducible component Z of Hilb_d(A^n_k,0) smoothable if Z is contained in R_d^n under the natural inclusion Hilb_d(A^n_k,0) subset Hilb_d(A^n_k). What can be said about these smoothable irreducible components of Hilb_d(A^n_k,0), and for fixed n and d how many such components are there?
justification: The draft clearly targets Problem XXIX in §2.7 rather than the earlier tangent-space problems. The official formulation there is essentially the same as your draft, so the main task is not to broaden it but to make its ambient notation explicit. The needed stand-alone definitions come from §1.3: the paper globally assumes an algebraically closed base field k, defines Hilb_d(X), and defines the punctual Hilbert scheme Hilb_d(A^n,0) as the fiber over d[0] of the Hilbert-Chow morphism, consisting of degree-d subschemes supported at 0. The phrase "smoothable component" is supplied in §2.1, where the smoothable component of Hilb_d(A^n) is defined as the closure of the locus of degree-d subschemes that are smooth. Problem XXIX then asks exactly for the structure and count of irreducible components of the punctual Hilbert scheme that lie inside that component. The sentence immediately after Problem XXIX explains a key motivation—there is, as far as the author knows, no natural injective map from components of the punctual Hilbert scheme to components of the full Hilbert scheme—but that remark is contextual rather than part of the formal problem, so it should not be folded into the refined question.
